lesson.title: One Sample or Two? Choosing the Right Design
lesson.summary: Whether to run a paired t-test or a two-sample t-test depends entirely on the study design, not on how the data happen to be arranged in a table, and choosing wrong can completely change the conclusion.
lesson.body:
Given two columns of numbers, should you treat them as one sample of differences (paired t-test) or as two independent samples (two-sample t-test)? Mixing this up is one of the most common errors in introductory statistics, and it is not just a technical slip, it can flip a study's conclusion entirely.

The test is about design, not appearance. Ask whether each observation in group 1 has a natural, non-arbitrary partner in group 2, for a reason connected to how the data were collected, not just because the numbers happen to sit on the same row of a spreadsheet. Before-and-after measurements on the same subject: pair them. Two different subjects who were deliberately matched on some trait expected to affect the outcome, such as twins, siblings, or patients matched by age and diagnosis, then split so each member of the pair gets a different treatment: pair them. Two separate groups of subjects who were sampled or assigned independently, with no such matching, such as 15 people randomly given Method A and a different, unrelated 12 people given Method B: treat them as independent samples, not pairs. One quick giveaway: paired data always has the same number of observations in each set, since it is fundamentally one sample of differences, while genuinely independent samples are allowed to have different sizes, as the n1 equals 15 and n2 equals 12 example in two-sample t-interval did.

The stakes of getting this wrong are easiest to see by making the mistake on purpose. Take the weight loss data from paired data, six people's weights before and after the program, and analyze it incorrectly as two independent samples instead. Before group: mean 186.667, standard deviation about 16.63. After group: mean 182.167, standard deviation about 16.46. Treating these as independent, the standard error is the square root of (276.67 divided by 6 plus 270.97 divided by 6), which is the square root of 46.11 plus 45.16, or the square root of 91.27, about 9.55. The test statistic becomes 4.5 divided by 9.55, about 0.47, nowhere near the critical value of 2.015 needed at df equals 5. That p-value is large, far from significant. Compare that to the correct paired analysis of the exact same 12 numbers from the previous section: t equals about 5.32, with a p-value below 0.005, overwhelmingly significant.

Same data, opposite conclusions. The independent-samples calculation drowns out the real effect because it ignores that each person's before and after weight are correlated, someone who starts heavier tends to still weigh more afterward, and that shared variation inflates the standard error enormously when it is not first removed by pairing. The lesson is not a minor technicality: pairing, when the design calls for it, is often the difference between detecting a real effect and completely missing it. Always ask how the data were collected before picking a procedure. Two columns of numbers never tell you the answer by themselves.
